name: Squall-Sabulum
description: Squall-Sabulum is a desert that has never known stillness. Its dust seas roll in slow bronze dunes from pole to pole, broken only by dead ocean basins where the water left a million years ago and salt crust gleams like glass. Above it all churns a permanent band of haboob storms, walls of grit two kilometers high that circle the equator and swallow the sun for weeks at a time.

When the squalls meet the mountain cold-fronts in the southern hemisphere, they wring out brief, vicious rains—dilute acid that hisses on the sandstone and leaves pitted runnels across the rock. Days scorch past 110 degrees; the same latitudes freeze hard after dark. The wind never stops talking, a low grinding hiss that miners say gets into dreams and stays there.

The Kestrel Deep Mining Complex was abandoned in a single afternoon when an uncharted squall line buried its main shaft and half its crew. The headframe still leans out of the dune field at an angle, and rescue beacons wired into the deep galleries occasionally flicker to life when storms short the old grid. Nobody has gone down to silence them.

Beneath the dust lies the fortune: titanium-rich paleoplacer deposits in those dead seabeds, plus aluminum and optical-grade silicon in the eroded highlands. Microbial mats bloom in the brine pockets under the salt flats, thriving on chemistry that would kill a human in minutes. Claim-jumpers and storm-chasing prospectors fight over the seabed leases every season, and every season the desert keeps a few of them.
